about.meta.description: Notes on how I got here. Design Engineer building design systems, tools, and digital products.
about.title: Notes on how I got here
about.p1: It all started with music. Before I knew what I wanted to do, I was obsessed with rhythm, layers, and tiny details, and that curiosity pulled me toward design: logos for bands, cover art, identities for creative projects. I've always been a computer kid too, so understanding how things are built was never far behind. Design isn't just what I do for work, it's something I care about deeply: how people use the tools around them, how technology integrates into daily life, what makes an experience feel smooth, accessible, and consistent. That's the thread connecting everything I've built.
about.p2: Today I work as a Design Engineer, after a path through product design, sitting at the intersection of both. Music runs in parallel as Marces, a project I'm looking forward to picking back up properly. Outside of work I'm deep into ergonomics and setup optimization (I will diagnose your desk uninvited), device and app reviews where tech meets music, and branding for fun, sometimes inventing projects just to give them an identity and bring them to life in code. I share that exploration through lemonims, my personal lab and small creative label.

case.mdds.title: Designed, engineered, and shipped. Solo.
case.mdds.subtitle: MDDS. Digital Memory Design System. Now running 110+ live instances in production, a quarter of them shipped by other devs.
case.mdds.overview.title: Three icon generations, directionless components. Zero system.
case.mdds.overview.p1: MDDS is the design system I built for ODILO's Archive & Preservation product. Before it existed, every screen defined its own buttons, notices, and icons: three generations of iconography coexisting, colors hardcoded in every stylesheet, and no shared visual language across modules. MDDS replaces all of that with a token layer, reusable components, and a unified icon library, now live in production.
case.mdds.overview.p2: But the most important change isn't visible on any screen: it's a new way of working. With solid foundations, every design decision stops being solved screen by screen and starts being solved once, in the right layer. That lets us tie the product together with more consistency for our clients, without repeating the same work in every module.
case.mdds.s1.title: Tokens first, screens later
case.mdds.s1.intro: The order matters as much as the outcome. Instead of creating components and retrofitting them to a token system, I followed the reverse sequence: tokens first, component second, documentation in parallel, migration last.
case.mdds.pipeline.title_sr: MDDS workflow pipeline: tokens, component, documentation, migration
case.mdds.s1.p1.title: Why that order.
case.mdds.s1.p1.body: Building a component before having tokens forces you to rewrite it as soon as the color or typography system changes. Starting with tokens forces you to answer the hard questions first: what's primitive, what's semantic, what depends on usage context. It ensures the component is born consuming variables, not loose values.
case.mdds.s1.p3.title: The Figma-to-code bridge.
case.mdds.s1.p3.body: Part of the work that isn't visible on any screen was connecting each token name in Figma with its CSS equivalent, so they would stop being maintained manually in two separate places. What's decided in design reaches code with the same name, no manual translation, no margin for error between tools.
case.mdds.s1.p4.title: How I approached each component.
case.mdds.s1.p4.body: I didn't design screens. I designed pieces the rest of the team could use without asking me for help. That meant accessibility and support for the application's six languages were built into each component from its first commit, not patched in later. And it meant documenting every variant in an internal playground, the team's working reference today, evolving toward a shareable internal product as the component set grows.
case.mdds.s2.title: From Figma to production, without manual translation
case.mdds.s2.p1: The pipeline extracts Figma variables and processes them to automatically generate the three token layers in CSS. What Figma doesn't handle well (edge cases, fine-tuning) is managed directly in code, without forcing the design tool to do something it wasn't built for.
case.mdds.s2.p2: Four components built from scratch with variants, states, and accessibility resolved within the component itself, not as an added layer. An icon library of 190+ icons unified into a single font, replacing three distinct icon generations. In production, used by public and private sector clients with strict accessibility requirements.
case.mdds.adoption.title_sr: MDDS component adoption by authorship: stacked bar chart showing percentage built by Andrea vs. the rest of the team
case.mdds.s2b.title: Documentation as a working session
case.mdds.s2b.p1: The playground isn't documentation written after the fact. It's shaped in continuous pairing with the company's senior frontend engineer (and mentor): what variants a component needs, how it handles edge cases, how a decision travels from Figma into code without losing intent. That shared review is what makes the system safe for other devs to build on without asking first. We're now extending it with agentic skills and workflows, so consuming a token or component gets even simpler for the rest of the team.
case.mdds.s2c.title: Where the friction was
case.mdds.s2c.p1: The hardest part wasn't technical. This product vertical had never had a design function. Early on, that meant defining acceptance criteria and handoffs from zero, iterating them with engineering as we went. As design engineer, the friction moved downstream: making each component robust enough to hold every variant a real screen throws at it, worked out directly with the senior frontend engineer before code ships. The value I add now lives in production, not in a handoff.
case.mdds.s3.title: Work that multiplies itself
case.mdds.s3.p1: Of the 110 live component instances in the product today, one in four was placed by another frontend team member, using components they didn't build. Once a component exists and is documented, the interface keeps improving without me intervening on every new screen. That's the effect a design system should have: work that multiplies itself.

case.mdds.stat1.label: design tokens (color, interface, typography)
case.mdds.stat2.label: icons in unified library, 60% originally authored
case.mdds.stat3.label: live instances from 4+ production components
case.mdds.stat4.label: of instances built by the rest of the team, without direct intervention
case.mdds.s5.title: What comes next
case.mdds.s5.p1: A brand or palette change now happens in the token layer, not screen by screen. Each new component builds on what's already there, so the next one comes together faster and lighter than the last. Table, navigation, and forms are next: they inherit tokens, icons, and a migration pattern already proven in production. Every migration also retires real technical debt, with a direct impact on both product velocity and the business bottom line. The system isn't finished. It's compounding.
case.linkims.title: A lightweight product that sacrifices neither design nor architecture.
case.linkims.subtitle: Linkims. Link-in-bio platform for Lemonims artists. In production since the first artist, with 0 production dependencies and a total bundle size of 18.2 KB.
case.linkims.overview.title: A Linktree doesn't represent a record label
case.linkims.overview.p1: Lemonims needed a centralized hub where each artist had a profile with links to their platforms: Spotify, YouTube, Instagram. Existing solutions like Linktree fell short on the only thing that mattered here: zero brand control, zero visual identity per artist, and a third party's branding on top of a product that represents a label.
case.linkims.overview.p2: The constraint wasn't technical, it was product: every profile has to feel like an extension of the artist's brand, not a generic template with swapped colors. That ruled out any solution based on predefined themes or surface-level configuration.
case.linkims.overview.p3: Today the hub hosts three profiles in production (my own, Marces, and Blanca Ferrer), with Blanca Ferrer serving as the edge case: its own serif typeface (Prociono), different weights, different CTA padding. All solved without touching the component CSS.
case.linkims.s1.title: The decision that defines everything else: no framework
case.linkims.s1.intro: Before any component or token, the first decision was architectural: vanilla TypeScript, no framework.
case.linkims.s1.p1.title: Why.
case.linkims.s1.p1.body: The product has no state, no reactivity, no composition at scale. These are static pages rendered from JSON. Adding a framework would have added ~40 KB of runtime to solve something that document.createElement covers in 227 lines. The result is a project with zero production dependencies, only 4 devDependencies for the build.
case.linkims.s1.p2.title: Tokens that adapt on their own.
case.linkims.s1.p2.body: Spacing (4px base), typography, radii, motion, and blur are defined as custom properties on :root. Tokens change at breakpoints, and the components consuming them adapt without additional CSS. The token is the contract between design and component: not a reference, a single source of truth.
case.linkims.s1.p3.title: One theme per artist, without touching components.
case.linkims.s1.p3.body: Each artist (.theme--marces, .theme--arodav, .theme--blanca-ferrer) overrides a set of custom properties: palette, gradient, typography, glass effects. Adding the complete visual identity of a new artist takes 6 custom properties, not a component rewrite.
case.linkims.s1.p4.title: The layout is also data, not code.
case.linkims.s1.p4.body: 6x5 CSS grid. Each card defines its position (row, col, rowSpan, colSpan) directly in the profile JSON, and TypeScript injects those coordinates as custom properties. Adding a new artist is a JSON file and an HTML file, not a development session.
case.linkims.s1.p5.title: Real multi-page, not a disguised SPA.
case.linkims.s1.p5.body: Four entry points in Vite. Each artist has their own index.html with dedicated <title>, meta tags, and favicon. Clean URLs (/arodav/), native SEO, no routing logic to maintain.
case.linkims.s2.title: The details that don't show in a diff
case.linkims.s2.intro: A product in production for real clients shows in what you don't see at first glance:
case.linkims.s2.p1: Double requestAnimationFrame on entry animations, to ensure the browser paints the initial state before firing the transition.
case.linkims.s2.p2: Animated favicon with the Page Visibility API: alternates colors every 2s when the tab is hidden, and clears the interval on return.
case.linkims.s2.p3: Icons via CSS mask + currentColor: they inherit the theme color automatically, no inline SVG to maintain per artist.
case.linkims.s2.p5: Progressive enhancement: semantic HTML works without JavaScript, with skip link, <nav>, ARIA labels, and lang attribute.
case.linkims.s2.outro: None of this was part of the brief. It's what separates a link-in-bio made for an artist from a generic template with a swapped logo.
case.linkims.s3.title: By the numbers
case.linkims.stat1.label: total minified bundle, with zero production dependencies
case.linkims.stat2.label: brand identities in production on a single component system
case.linkims.stat3.label: custom properties needed to onboard a new artist's complete visual identity
case.linkims.stat4.label: ARIA attributes and skip links, accessibility solved from the ground up
case.linkims.s4.title: What this unlocks
case.linkims.s4.p1: Adding a new artist to Lemonims is no longer a project: it's a profile JSON and an index.html. The token system absorbs the visual identity without touching a component, and edge cases (like Blanca Ferrer) are solved with custom properties, not CSS forks.
case.linkims.s4.p2: This first version is deliberately an MVP: the token architecture already proves that a complete theme reduces to a handful of variables, but that tuning is still done by me, by hand, for each artist. The next step isn't optimizing that process, it's eliminating it as a bottleneck: turning the same token system into a configurable product, with a panel where each artist can adjust their own design within a system with thoughtful constraints, not a free editor that breaks visual coherence.
case.linkims.s4.p3: It's the difference between an internal tool for Lemonims and a product any independent artist can use to have an online presence with their own identity, not just another template. The technical foundation (tokens as contract, themes as data, zero dependencies) is already in place to support that leap without rewriting.
